cells.tense: You know which chapter is done, and you end it on purpose.
cells.ask: Close one loop out loud today — tell someone a thing is finished, name what it gave you, then leave the space open rather than filling it.
cells.core:
You can feel when something is over before anyone says it. So the finishing gets done on time, and the space it leaves gets treated as space, not as a hole to fill. That's the exchange working: you give the old thing its ending and you take the room it makes.

Fairness rides along with it naturally. You're not keeping score on who ended what or who owes what — you just know what's even and you act like it. What this is free to feed next is a start that isn't weighed down by anything left unclosed. Most people drag the last thing in with them. You've learned how to actually set one down.
cells.sheetLine: You end things on purpose, and the space it leaves gets to stay open.
cells.verb: letting what is finished end so the new thing can start
cells.place: standing at the threshold where an ending is clearing space for a beginning

cells.tense: You will end this before it has finished pouring itself out.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you were about to close and give it one more full week, deciding nothing in it until the week is up. Then decide.
cells.core:
Endings are coming faster than they're needed, and the speed has started to feel like freedom. Somewhere ahead is the cleaner life this is supposed to produce, so anything unfinished reads as a delay to cut — plans, rooms, jobs, people, often several at once. Tearing something down feels like motion, so it keeps getting chosen over the slower thing.

A real ending draws its force from being necessary, and something that hasn't had room to grow can't be necessary yet. You find out what you were mid-way through by staying one more inch. The hard part isn't letting go. It's staying long enough for letting go to mean something.
cells.sheetLine: You end things early and call it freedom.
cells.verb: letting what is finished end so the new thing can start

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that has already shut.
cells.ask: Do one small closing act on something finished — return the thing, delete the folder, say the last sentence out loud — and stop there.
cells.core:
You're holding on to something that's already over. Not because you haven't noticed — you keep it, and the keeping has started to read as steady rather than as held. So the finished thing stays in the room and takes up the space a new one would need.

Nothing here is missing. Plenty of energy lives in you, pointed at whatever's in front of you. That direction is already yours; the closing is the part being withheld — keeping the old thing safe from the very decision that would finish it. Even one small close returns something. These endings aren't loss. They're the ground clearing.
cells.sheetLine: You're protecting something that's already finished from the ending it needs.
cells.verb: letting what is finished end so the new thing can start

cells.tense: Something in you is already ending while you describe it as steady.
cells.ask: Write down the one thing you keep describing as fine when you talk about it, then read what you wrote and say out loud whether it is.
cells.core:
Something is changing shape in your life right now and you haven't named it that way. You keep saying things are steady, and by every measure you can point to they are — while something in the middle of you has already stopped being what it was.

That doesn't mean you're scared or hiding. It means the change is early and hasn't announced itself. The ending is running on its own. Naming it doesn't decide when anything stops — it decides whether you're the one steering or the one who finds out afterward. Say something here and you're back at the front of it.
cells.sheetLine: Something is already ending while you call it steady.
